title.en: Four shapes and a wise star

text.en: Circle, Square, Triangle and Rectangle are friends, but one day each claims to be the best. They ask a wise star to decide. She tells them that together they can make the most beautiful pictures and patterns. This chapter is about shapes, friendship and the small words a and an.

Four friends, Circle, Square, Triangle and Rectangle, begin to fight about who is the best. Circle says she is round and beautiful with no sharp edges, and children use her to draw a smiling face. Square says he has four equal sides, and many sweets are square. Triangle says she has three sides, and children use her to draw mountains. Rectangle says he has four sides, two long and two short, and many biscuits and chocolates are rectangles.
The friends cannot decide, so they agree to ask the first person they meet. They meet a star. The wise star says they are all friends and should not fight. She tells them that together they can create the most beautiful pictures and patterns. The friends realise their mistake, promise never to fight again and remain best friends forever. The lesson is that everyone is special in their own way, and we do more wonderful things together than alone.
A circle is round and has no sharp edges or corners. A square has four sides that are all equal. A triangle has three sides. A rectangle has four straight sides and four square corners. Its opposite sides are the same length. A square is a rectangle with all four sides equal. Look around you: a wheel is a circle, a window can be a rectangle, a roof can be a triangle and a tile can be a square.
We use a before a singular noun that begins with a consonant sound, such as a dog, a cow and a sparrow. We use an before a singular naming word that starts with a vowel sound. Listen to the beginning of eagle, umbrella and ice cream: an eagle, an umbrella and an ice cream. The vowels are a, e, i, o and u. All the other letters are consonants. So we say a brown hen laid an egg.
To write about a friend, tell the name, whether a boy or a girl, the age, the favourite colour, the game the friend likes and what the friend wants to become. A good friend helps us, shares with us and does not fight over small things.

If the star asks the friends to draw a school, which shapes could they use for the roof, the wall and a round clock?

board.text: A roof | a wall | a clock

text.en: A triangle can make the roof, a rectangle can make the wall, and a circle can make the clock. The picture uses each shape for a different job.
Work with a friend to plan another picture. Ask what your friend wants to add, then explain what your own shape can do in the same picture.
Look at two shapes with four square corners. Measure their sides. One can have two pairs of equal sides while the other has all four sides equal.
The one with all four sides equal is a square. Turn it so one tip points up. It is still a square because turning it does not change its sides or corners.

board.text: Turn the square | sides stay equal

text.en: Listen to orange and bag before you write. Orange starts with a vowel sound, so say an orange. Bag starts with a consonant sound, so say a bag.
Now listen to hour and uniform. The h in hour is silent, so we say an hour. Uniform starts with a y sound, so we say a uniform.
Add a describing word: a green apple. The first sound after a is the g in green. Take green away and we say an apple.
Write a sentence about something you and a friend like to do. Read it aloud and, if you used a or an, listen to the sound that comes next.

board.text: Write → read aloud → check the next sound

problem.en: Fill in a or an: ___ eagle sat on ___ building.

text.en: Eagle begins with the vowel e.
Building begins with the consonant b.
An eagle sat on a building.

problem.en: Fill in a or an: ___ apricot and ___ chikoo.

text.en: Apricot begins with the vowel a.
Chikoo begins with the consonant c.
An apricot and a chikoo.

prompt.en: Say what the star taught the shapes.

commonMisconceptions.en: One shape is truly the best

points.en: Circle, Square, Triangle and Rectangle each thought they were best.
Together the shapes make beautiful pictures and patterns.
A circle has no corners, a square has four equal sides, a triangle has three sides.
Use a before consonant sounds and an before vowel sounds.
Friends should not fight; together they do wonders.
